newsitem.title: USA: Mars probe to lead fleet to Red Planet.
newsitem.headline: Mars probe to lead fleet to Red Planet.

text.p: Mars Global Surveyor, the first in an international armada of spacecraft bound for the Red Planet, was set for blastoff on Wednesday, U.S. space agency officials said.
A McDonnell Douglas Corp. Delta 2 rocket was to soar aloft with the one-tonne Mars probe from Cape Canaveral Air Station at 12:11 p.m. EST (1711 GMT).

Mars Global Surveyor is the first in a trio of space probes due to be dispatched to the Red Planet this year. It will be followed on Nov. 16 by Russia's Mars 96, an orbiter carrying 12 instruments, two small landers and two spike-like surface penetrators. And a second U.S. craft, Mars Pathfinder, scheduled for launch on Dec. 2 consists of a landing station and a small robotic rover called Sojourner.
NASA plans to send additional pairs of spacecraft to Mars every 26 months through 2005.

"We inaugurate this year a series of missions designed to explore planet Mars in detail," Wesley Huntress, NASA's head of space science, said. "We can systematically pry loose the secrets of Mars: its origins and its history."

The Mars Global Surveyor was designed, built and prepared for launch in record time as a replacement for NASA's $1 billion Mars Observer probe, which spun out of control just days before it was due to reach the planet in 1993. Surveyor carries copies of five of the seven scientific instruments on the Observer, but at $215 million it is much cheaper.

"It has 80 percent of the science of the Mars Observer at one-quarter the cost," NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin said. "It's a very, very strong statement about the will of the NASA people to do more with less."

If all goes according to plan, Surveyor will enter an egg-shaped orbit around Mars in September 1997. It will lower and circularize its orbit by dipping into the thin Martian atmosphere and using its wing-like solar panels as brakes.

By March 1998, the spacecraft will be positioned to begin its study of the planet. The rugged Martian surface of flood plains, towering volcanoes and canyons will come under closer scrutiny than ever before as the spacecraft orbits over the planet's ice-covered polar caps.
From 230 miles (367 km) up, the probe's camera will see objects on the surface as small as a compact car.

By the end of one Martian year, 687 Earth days, most of the planet will have been mapped by the Surveyor's electronic eye. A wide-angle camera will provide daily weather pictures and other instruments will attempt to detect water and determine the composition of the rocky surface.
Much of the data beamed back from Surveyor will be used to scout out landing sites for future robotic missions to Mars, some of which may return samples of Martian rock to earth.
